PgBouncer in transaction mode can't handle prepared statements, so the driver must be configured with `prepare: false`. We added it to pool.ts and the options type in driver.ts, but driver.ts still doesn't pass it to the raw pool, so it isn't taking effect yet.
Action: Pass `prepare: false` through to the raw pool in driver.ts and add a test.

I don't have that gotcha on record, and I'd rather not guess which pooler quirk it is. Post-deploy error bursts through a pooler are often prepared-statement or stale-connection issues, but I can't confirm that's ours. Action: read the db client config and the pooler settings to see what the driver is configured for, and check the git log for a note on it.

PgBouncer runs in transaction mode, so prepared statements must be disabled in the driver (prepare: false). The burst after deploys is likely new connections re-preparing statements that land on a different server connection. Action: check where the db client is created in the api and worker and confirm prepare: false is set on both.

The hydration warning is the due date being formatted in the server's timezone on render (12:42 PM) and the browser's on the client (8:42 AM), so I'd format with an explicit timeZone or render that cell client-side only.

A readiness probe is the one that fixes your problem, since it keeps pods out of the Service until they can actually serve; liveness restarts stuck ones, and I'd consider a startupProbe too if boot is slow. I don't know the health endpoint or port yet, so I'll check instead of guessing.

The health endpoint GET /healthz checks Postgres and Redis, which is right for readiness, so traffic only reaches pods that can serve. I'd not use it for liveness, because a DB or Redis blip would make Kubernetes restart every pod. Action: read the api chart's deployment template and values, add a readinessProbe on /healthz, and add a liveness probe against a lightweight check (I'll see if one exists, otherwise propose adding it), then run helm lint and helm template.

Readiness can use GET /healthz on port 4000, which returns 200 only when Postgres and Redis are both up. For liveness I'd avoid that endpoint if we can, since a db blip would restart every pod; a lighter check or a generous failureThreshold is safer. Action: edit the api chart in infra/helm/api (deployment template plus values.yaml and values-prod.yaml) to add readinessProbe, livenessProbe and a startupProbe, then run helm lint and helm template to check it renders.
